claim: Social isolation generally increases aggression in animal models.
source: Social isolation also increases male aggression in mice (Matsumoto et al., 2005; Zelikowsky et al., 2018) and even in humans (Ferguson et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies in mice and humans showing increased aggression with social isolation.

claim: Social isolation increases lunging frequency in Drosophila males.
source: Consistently, it has been found that social isolation increases lunging frequency (Palavicino-Maggio and Sengupta, 2022; Yadav et al., 2024) by altering the expression of genes such as Cyp6a20 (Wang et al., 2008), Drosulfakinin (Dsk) (Agrawal et al., 2020), and Tachykinin (Tk) (Asahina et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies demonstrating increased lunging with social isolation.

claim: Social enrichment increases male mating success in Drosophila.
source: Meanwhile, social enrichment increases male mating success by enhancing the sensitivity of Or47b-expressing olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) to fly pheromones common to both sexes (Lin et al., 2016; Sethi et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies showing enhanced Or47b ORN sensitivity and increased mating success with social enrichment.

claim: Group-housed males show higher frequency of tussling behavior compared to 2-day-old males in the presence of an embedded virgin female.
source: We found that males who were group-housed for 7 days showed a significantly higher frequency of tussling behavior and reduced latency to tussle in the presence of an embedded virgin female (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B comparing tussling behavior across different conditions.

claim: 14-day-old group-housed males show a higher proportion of tussling behavior compared to 7-day-old males.
source: We observed a significantly higher proportion of 14-day-old males raised in groups that showed tussling behavior during the 2 hr observation period, compared to the 7-day-old males (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1B showing age-dependent differences in tussling.

claim: 2-day-old males never display tussling behavior.
source: Furthermore, 2-day-old males never displayed tussling behavior.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations of 2-day-old males.

claim: 14-day-old males show lower levels of lunging behavior than 7-day-old males.
source: In contrast, 14-day-old males showed a lower level of lunging behavior than 7-day-old males did (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 comparing lunging across ages.

claim: Male tussling intensity increases significantly with higher yeast concentrations in food.
source: On the contrary, male tussling intensity increased significantly with higher yeast concentrations such that more than 70% of males displayed this high-intensity fighting behavior (Figure 1D, see Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1D showing dose-dependent effects of yeast on tussling.

claim: Sucrose concentration in food has no effect on male tussling behavior.
source: We found that these males displayed similar levels of tussling behavior with different concentrations of sucrose in the food (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1C showing no significant differences across sucrose concentrations.

claim: Group-housed males perform less frequent lunging behavior in 10 min than single-housed males.
source: Interestingly, we found that while SH males performed more frequent lunging behavior in 10 min than GH males did, which is consistent with previous findings, they rarely showed tussling behavior.
evidence: Supported by experimental comparison between single-housed and group-housed males.

claim: Single-housed males rarely show tussling behavior.
source: Interestingly, we found that while SH males performed more frequent lunging behavior in 10 min than GH males did, which is consistent with previous findings, they rarely showed tussling behavior.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations of single-housed males.

claim: Group-housed males display a large number of tussling events within 2 hr.
source: In contrast, GH males displayed a large number of tussling events within 2 hr (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B comparing tussling events.

claim: Group-housed males exhibit reduced tussling latency compared to single-housed males.
source: Statistical analysis of tussling and lunging behaviors showed that GH males exhibited reduced tussling latency and enhanced tussling frequency, in addition to increased lunging latency and decreased lunging frequency, compared to SH males (Figure 2C–F).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figures 2C-F.

claim: Group-housed males exhibit enhanced tussling frequency compared to single-housed males.
source: Statistical analysis of tussling and lunging behaviors showed that GH males exhibited reduced tussling latency and enhanced tussling frequency, in addition to increased lunging latency and decreased lunging frequency, compared to SH males (Figure 2C–F).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figures 2C-F.

claim: Group-housed males exhibit increased lunging latency compared to single-housed males.
source: Statistical analysis of tussling and lunging behaviors showed that GH males exhibited reduced tussling latency and enhanced tussling frequency, in addition to increased lunging latency and decreased lunging frequency, compared to SH males (Figure 2C–F).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figures 2C-F.

claim: Group-housed males exhibit decreased lunging frequency compared to single-housed males.
source: Statistical analysis of tussling and lunging behaviors showed that GH males exhibited reduced tussling latency and enhanced tussling frequency, in addition to increased lunging latency and decreased lunging frequency, compared to SH males (Figure 2C–F).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figures 2C-F.

claim: The average duration of individual lunging events is less than 0.2 seconds.
source: We also quantified the duration of each tussling and lunging event and found that the average duration of individual lunging events was less than 0.2 s, while a tussling event lasted from seconds to minutes (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of event durations shown in Figure 2G.

claim: A tussling event lasts from seconds to minutes.
source: We also quantified the duration of each tussling and lunging event and found that the average duration of individual lunging events was less than 0.2 s, while a tussling event lasted from seconds to minutes (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of event durations shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Tussling is a more intense form of aggressive behavior compared to lunging.
source: This further suggests that tussling is a more intense form of aggressive behavior compared to lunging.
evidence: Inferred from the duration data showing tussling lasts much longer than lunging.

claim: Social enrichment inhibits low-intensity lunging in male flies.
source: These results indicate that social enrichment inhibits low-intensity lunging but promotes high-intensity tussling in male flies.
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing single-housed and group-housed males.

claim: Social enrichment promotes high-intensity tussling in male flies.
source: These results indicate that social enrichment inhibits low-intensity lunging but promotes high-intensity tussling in male flies.
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing single-housed and group-housed males.

claim: Or67d ORNs mediate acute cVA stimulation and promote male aggression.
source: Two cVA sensory neurons, Or67d and Or65a ORNs, play crucial roles in enhancing the lunging-based aggression in SH males, in which Or67d ORNs mediate acute cVA stimulation and promote male aggression (Wang and Anderson, 2010), while Or65a ORNs mediate chronic cVA stimulation and inhibit male aggression in GH males (Liu et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang and Anderson, 2010 study.

claim: Or65a ORNs mediate chronic cVA stimulation and inhibit male aggression in group-housed males.
source: Two cVA sensory neurons, Or67d and Or65a ORNs, play crucial roles in enhancing the lunging-based aggression in SH males, in which Or67d ORNs mediate acute cVA stimulation and promote male aggression (Wang and Anderson, 2010), while Or65a ORNs mediate chronic cVA stimulation and inhibit male aggression in GH males (Liu et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2011 study.

claim: Silencing Or47b ORNs significantly decreases male tussling behavior.
source: We found that silencing Or47b ORNs, but not Or67d, Or65a, or Ir84a ORNs, significantly decreased male tussling, compared to the control (Figure 3A and B, see Supplementary file 1 for detailed genotypes).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from silencing experiments shown in Figures 3A and B.

claim: Silencing Or67d ORNs significantly reduces male lunging behavior.
source: In contrast, silencing Or67d ORNs, but not other ORNs, significantly reduced male lunging (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from silencing experiments shown in Figures 3C and D.

claim: Or47b ORNs mediate male tussling behavior.
source: These loss-of-function results suggest that Or47b ORNs mediate male tussling behavior, whereas Or67d ORNs regulate male lunging behavior.
evidence: Inferred from loss-of-function experiments showing specific effects of Or47b silencing on tussling.

claim: Or67d ORNs regulate male lunging behavior.
source: These loss-of-function results suggest that Or47b ORNs mediate male tussling behavior, whereas Or67d ORNs regulate male lunging behavior.
evidence: Inferred from loss-of-function experiments showing specific effects of Or67d silencing on lunging.

claim: Knocking down Or47b receptor expression significantly decreases male tussling behavior.
source: Our results showed a significant decrease in male tussling behavior when the Or47b receptor expression was reduced (Figure 3E and F), indicating that the functionality of Or47b ORNs in tussling is dependent on the Or47b receptor.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from RNAi knockdown experiments shown in Figures 3E and F.

claim: The functionality of Or47b ORNs in tussling is dependent on the Or47b receptor.
source: Our results showed a significant decrease in male tussling behavior when the Or47b receptor expression was reduced (Figure 3E and F), indicating that the functionality of Or47b ORNs in tussling is dependent on the Or47b receptor.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental result that Or47b knockdown reduces tussling.

claim: Or47b plays a more crucial role than FruM in mediating male tussling.
source: We observed a slight increase in tussling latency in fruM knocked-down males, although not significantly different from the control (Figure 3E and F), suggesting that Or47b, rather than FruM, plays a more crucial role in mediating male tussling.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of Or47b and fruM knockdown effects on tussling.

claim: Single-housed males with enhanced activity of Or47b ORNs show a significant increase in tussling behavior compared to control single-housed males.
source: We found that these SH males with enhanced activity of Or47b ORNs showed a significant increase in tussling behavior compared to control SH males.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from optogenetic activation experiments.

claim: The level of tussling in single-housed males with activated Or47b ORNs is indistinguishable from that in group-housed males.
source: Interestingly, the level of tussling in these SH males with activated Or47b ORNs was indistinguishable from that in GH males (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing activated single-housed males to group-housed males shown in Figures 3G and H.

claim: Social enrichment acts through Or47b ORNs to promote male tussling.
source: These gain-of-function results indicate that social enrichment acts through Or47b ORNs to promote male tussling.
evidence: Inferred from gain-of-function experiments showing Or47b activation mimics social enrichment effects.

claim: There are substantially more downstream signals of Or47b ORNs in group-housed males than in single-housed males.
source: Using the trans-Tango technique that labels downstream neurons through ligand-receptor mediated signaling (Talay et al., 2017), we found substantially more downstream signals of Or47b ORNs in GH males than those in SH males (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), suggesting the involvement of Or47b ORNs under social enrichment.
evidence: Supported by trans-Tango labeling data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Silencing mushroom body neurons does not affect male tussling.
source: We found that silencing the mushroom body neurons by expressing an inwardly rectifying potassium channel Kir2.1 (Baines et al., 2001) driven by R19B03-GAL4 did not affect male tussling, suggesting that the experience-dependent tussling behavior is not dependent on the classical learning and memory center.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from silencing mushroom body neurons.

claim: Experience-dependent tussling behavior is not dependent on the classical learning and memory center.
source: We found that silencing the mushroom body neurons by expressing an inwardly rectifying potassium channel Kir2.1 (Baines et al., 2001) driven by R19B03-GAL4 did not affect male tussling, suggesting that the experience-dependent tussling behavior is not dependent on the classical learning and memory center.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of effect when mushroom body neurons are silenced.

claim: Inactivation of P1a neurons does not affect tussling behavior.
source: Surprisingly, inactivation of the previously identified aggression-promoting P1a and TK neurons did not affect tussling behavior (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from inactivation experiments shown in Figures 4A and B.

claim: Inactivation of TK neurons does not affect tussling behavior.
source: Surprisingly, inactivation of the previously identified aggression-promoting P1a and TK neurons did not affect tussling behavior (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from inactivation experiments shown in Figures 4A and B.

claim: The central circuit for tussling behavior may be distinct from the previously reported aggression circuits.
source: These results imply that the central circuit for tussling behavior may be distinct from the previously reported aggression circuits.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of effect when P1a and TK neurons are inactivated.

claim: Inactivation of pC1SS2 neurons significantly reduces tussling behavior in male flies.
source: We found that inactivation of pC1SS2 but not pC1SS1 neurons significantly reduced the tussling behavior in male flies (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from inactivation experiments shown in Figures 4A and B.

claim: pC1SS2 neurons may be key central neurons regulating tussling behavior.
source: These results suggest that pC1SS2 neurons may be key central neurons regulating tussling behavior.
evidence: Inferred from the significant reduction in tussling when pC1SS2 neurons are inactivated.

claim: Optogenetic activation of P1a neurons induces acute courtship behavior as indicated by unilateral wing extension.
source: Compared to control male pairs that did not show any significant change upon red light stimulation (Figure 4F–H), optogenetic activation of P1a neurons induced acute courtship behavior as indicated by unilateral wing extension (UWE), and upon red light removal, there was a significant increase in lunging but not tussling (Figure 4I–K), consistent with previous findings.
evidence: Supported by optogenetic activation data shown in Figures 4I-K.

claim: Upon red light removal after P1a activation, there is a significant increase in lunging but not tussling.
source: Compared to control male pairs that did not show any significant change upon red light stimulation (Figure 4F–H), optogenetic activation of P1a neurons induced acute courtship behavior as indicated by unilateral wing extension (UWE), and upon red light removal, there was a significant increase in lunging but not tussling (Figure 4I–K), consistent with previous findings.
evidence: Supported by optogenetic activation data shown in Figures 4I-K.

claim: Optogenetic activation of pC1SS2 neurons induces strong and acute tussling behavior.
source: In contrast, optogenetic activation of pC1SS2 neurons induced strong and acute tussling behavior, with more than 50% of the time during red light in tussling, and the tussling behavior ceased immediately upon removal of red light (Figure 4L, see Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic activation data shown in Figure 4L.

claim: Tussling behavior ceases immediately upon removal of red light after pC1SS2 activation.
source: In contrast, optogenetic activation of pC1SS2 neurons induced strong and acute tussling behavior, with more than 50% of the time during red light in tussling, and the tussling behavior ceased immediately upon removal of red light (Figure 4L, see Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic activation data shown in Figure 4L.

claim: Activation of pC1SS2 neurons does not significantly affect male lunging.
source: Activation of pC1SS2 neurons did not significantly affect either male lunging or courtship (Figure 4M and N).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic activation data shown in Figures 4M and N.

claim: Activation of pC1SS2 neurons does not significantly affect male courtship.
source: Activation of pC1SS2 neurons did not significantly affect either male lunging or courtship (Figure 4M and N).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic activation data shown in Figures 4M and N.

claim: pC1SS2 neurons acutely promote high-intensity tussling behavior.
source: These results indicate that pC1SS2 neurons acutely promote the high-intensity tussling behavior.
evidence: Inferred from optogenetic activation experiments showing immediate tussling upon pC1SS2 activation.

claim: Thermal activation of P1a neurons at 30°C induces male tussling.
source: We found that activation of P1a neurons via dTrpA1 at 30°C induced male tussling, just like activation of pC1SS2 neurons did (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by thermal activation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Thermal activation of pC1SS2 neurons at 30°C induces male tussling.
source: We found that activation of P1a neurons via dTrpA1 at 30°C induced male tussling, just like activation of pC1SS2 neurons did (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by thermal activation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Vision is a key factor for P1a-induced tussling.
source: As thermal activation but not optogenetic activation of P1a neurons induced tussling, we reasoned that vision might be a key factor for this discrepancy, since all optogenetic experiments were performed in dark or red light.
evidence: Inferred from the discrepancy between thermal and optogenetic activation results.

claim: Activation of pC1SS2 but not P1a neurons induces tussling in dark.
source: Thus, we re-performed these thermal activation experiments in dark and found that activation of pC1SS2 but not P1a neurons induced tussling, although the level of tussling by pC1SS2-activated males was lower compared to that in light, suggesting a crucial role of vision in male tussling.
evidence: Supported by thermal activation experiments performed in dark conditions.

claim: Vision plays a crucial role in male tussling.
source: Thus, we re-performed these thermal activation experiments in dark and found that activation of pC1SS2 but not P1a neurons induced tussling, although the level of tussling by pC1SS2-activated males was lower compared to that in light, suggesting a crucial role of vision in male tussling.
evidence: Inferred from the reduced tussling in dark compared to light conditions.

claim: P1a neurons can promote both lunging and tussling behaviors, but their function on tussling requires visual stimulation.
source: These optogenetic and thermogenetic activation experiments suggest that P1a neurons can promote both lunging and tussling behaviors, but their function on tussling requires visual stimulation, while pC1SS2 neurons play a more direct role in acutely promoting male tussling.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of optogenetic and thermogenetic activation results under different lighting conditions.

claim: pC1SS2 neurons play a more direct role in acutely promoting male tussling.
source: These optogenetic and thermogenetic activation experiments suggest that P1a neurons can promote both lunging and tussling behaviors, but their function on tussling requires visual stimulation, while pC1SS2 neurons play a more direct role in acutely promoting male tussling.
evidence: Inferred from the immediate and consistent tussling response to pC1SS2 activation.

claim: Most P1a neurons are fru-positive and dsx-positive.
source: We found that most P1a neurons were fru-positive and dsx-positive, while pC1SS2 neurons were dsx-positive but fru-negative (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figures 5A-D.

claim: pC1SS2 neurons are dsx-positive but fru-negative.
source: We found that most P1a neurons were fru-positive and dsx-positive, while pC1SS2 neurons were dsx-positive but fru-negative (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figures 5A-D.

claim: dsx instead of fru may play crucial roles in the development and function of pC1SS2 neurons.
source: These results suggest that dsx instead of fru may play crucial roles in the development and function of pC1SS2 neurons.
evidence: Inferred from the expression pattern showing pC1SS2 neurons are dsx-positive but fru-negative.

claim: dsxM knockdown in pC1SS2 neurons slightly increases the number of cells from two to three pairs to three to four pairs.
source: We found that dsxM knockdown in pC1SS2 neurons slightly increased the number of cells from two to three pairs to three to four pairs (Figure 5E–G), and significantly lengthened the axonal projections ventrally (Figure 5H).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figures 5E-G.

claim: dsxM knockdown in pC1SS2 neurons significantly lengthens the axonal projections ventrally.
source: We found that dsxM knockdown in pC1SS2 neurons slightly increased the number of cells from two to three pairs to three to four pairs (Figure 5E–G), and significantly lengthened the axonal projections ventrally (Figure 5H).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Males with dsx knocked down in pC1SS2 neurons show no tussling behavior during the first activation session.
source: However, males with dsx knocked down in pC1SS2 neurons showed no tussling behavior during the first activation session and few tussling behaviors during the second activation session (Figure 5J and K).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic activation data shown in Figures 5J and K.

claim: Males with dsx knocked down in pC1SS2 neurons show few tussling behaviors during the second activation session.
source: However, males with dsx knocked down in pC1SS2 neurons showed no tussling behavior during the first activation session and few tussling behaviors during the second activation session (Figure 5J and K).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic activation data shown in Figures 5J and K.

claim: dsx gene plays a crucial role in the development and tussling-promoting function of pC1SS2 neurons.
source: Together, these results reveal the crucial role of the dsx gene in the development and tussling-promoting function of pC1SS2 neurons.
evidence: Inferred from the developmental and functional deficits observed when dsx is knocked down in pC1SS2 neurons.

claim: 14-day-old group-housed males have a significant advantage over 14-day-old single-housed males in territorial control.
source: We further found that while GH 7-day-old males (G7) won slightly, but not significantly, more than SH 7-day-old males (S7) (Figure 6B), older G14 males had a significant advantage over the S14 males (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 2, and Figure 6—video 1).
evidence: Supported by territorial control test data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: 7-day-old group-housed males win slightly, but not significantly, more than 7-day-old single-housed males in territorial control.
source: We further found that while GH 7-day-old males (G7) won slightly, but not significantly, more than SH 7-day-old males (S7) (Figure 6B), older G14 males had a significant advantage over the S14 males (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 2, and Figure 6—video 1).
evidence: Supported by territorial control test data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: 14-day-old group-housed males display a significantly increased mating advantage over 14-day-old single-housed males.
source: We found that G7 males had no significant advantage over S7 males (Figure 6E); however, G14 males displayed a significantly increased mating advantage over S14 males (Figure 6F, see Figure 6—video 2).
evidence: Supported by mating competition test data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: 7-day-old group-housed males have no significant advantage over 7-day-old single-housed males in mating competition.
source: We found that G7 males had no significant advantage over S7 males (Figure 6E); however, G14 males displayed a significantly increased mating advantage over S14 males (Figure 6F, see Figure 6—video 2).
evidence: Supported by mating competition test data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Tussling-favored group-housed males are more competitive in territory control and mating compared to lunging-favored single-housed males.
source: Together, these results suggest that the tussling-favored GH males are more competitive in territory control and mating compared to the lunging-favored SH males, supporting a correlation between tussling and reproductive competition.
evidence: Inferred from the territorial control and mating competition results.

claim: There is a correlation between tussling and reproductive competition.
source: Together, these results suggest that the tussling-favored GH males are more competitive in territory control and mating compared to the lunging-favored SH males, supporting a correlation between tussling and reproductive competition.
evidence: Inferred from the association between tussling behavior and competitive success.

claim: Younger males have a greater mating advantage compared to older males under the same rearing conditions.
source: The results showed that younger males, whether reared in group or isolation, had a greater mating advantage compared to older males (G7 >G14, S7 >S14, G14 >G21, S14 >S21; Figure 6G, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by mating competition test data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: There is generally a disadvantage in mating competition associated with aging.
source: These results indicate that there is generally a disadvantage in mating competition associated with aging.
evidence: Inferred from the consistent pattern of younger males outcompeting older males.

claim: 21-day-old group-housed males are significantly more competitive than 14-day-old single-housed males in mating competition.
source: We found that while 14-day-old males were less competitive than 7-day-old males regardless of the rearing condition, indicative of the aging-related disadvantage, 21-day-old GH males were significantly more competitive than 14-day-old SH males (G21 >S14; Figure 6H).
evidence: Supported by mating competition test data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Males with inactivated Or47b neurons are incompetent for both territorial control and mating competition compared to control males.
source: We found that males with inactivated Or47b or pC1SS2 neurons were incompetent for both territorial control and mating competition compared to control males (Figure 6—figure supplement 3), further supporting a correlation between the occurrence of tussling behavior and the acquisition of territorial and mating competition advantages.
evidence: Supported by territorial control and mating competition test data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Males with inactivated pC1SS2 neurons are incompetent for both territorial control and mating competition compared to control males.
source: We found that males with inactivated Or47b or pC1SS2 neurons were incompetent for both territorial control and mating competition compared to control males (Figure 6—figure supplement 3), further supporting a correlation between the occurrence of tussling behavior and the acquisition of territorial and mating competition advantages.
evidence: Supported by territorial control and mating competition test data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: There is a correlation between the occurrence of tussling behavior and the acquisition of territorial and mating competition advantages.
source: We found that males with inactivated Or47b or pC1SS2 neurons were incompetent for both territorial control and mating competition compared to control males (Figure 6—figure supplement 3), further supporting a correlation between the occurrence of tussling behavior and the acquisition of territorial and mating competition advantages.
evidence: Inferred from the loss of competitive advantages when tussling-promoting neurons are inactivated.

claim: Long-term social enrichment in older males increases their territorial and mating competition.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that long-term social enrichment in older males increases their territorial and mating competition, which can overcome their mating disadvantage associated with aging (Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by the combined results from territorial control and mating competition tests.

claim: Social enrichment can overcome mating disadvantage associated with aging in males.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that long-term social enrichment in older males increases their territorial and mating competition, which can overcome their mating disadvantage associated with aging (Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by the finding that 21-day-old group-housed males outcompete 14-day-old single-housed males.

claim: Lunges are insufficient to establish dominance but mainly serve to maintain social status.
source: A recent work showed that lunges are insufficient to establish dominance but mainly serve to maintain social status, while tussling frequency is correlated with dominance establishment (Simon and Heberlein, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Simon and Heberlein, 2020 study.

claim: Tussling frequency is correlated with dominance establishment.
source: A recent work showed that lunges are insufficient to establish dominance but mainly serve to maintain social status, while tussling frequency is correlated with dominance establishment (Simon and Heberlein, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Simon and Heberlein, 2020 study.

claim: The male-specific volatile pheromone 11-cis-vaccenyl acetate (cVA) acutely promotes lunging behavior via its olfactory receptor Or67d.
source: In particular, the male-specific volatile pheromone 11-cis-vaccenyl acetate (cVA) acutely promotes lunging behavior via its olfactory receptor Or67d (Wang and Anderson, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang and Anderson, 2010 study.

claim: Chronic cVA exposure in socially enriched males reduces the level of lunging via olfactory receptor Or65a.
source: Interestingly, chronic cVA exposure in socially enriched males reduces the level of lunging via another olfactory receptor Or65a (Liu et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2011 study.

claim: Artificially activating Or47b ORNs improves mating advantage in a competitive assay.
source: Artificially activating Or47b ORNs also improves mating advantage in a competitive assay (Dweck et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dweck et al., 2015 study.

claim: Group housing and age-dependent juvenile hormone jointly increase the expression of male-specific proteins from fruitless (fruM) in Or47b-expressing ORNs.
source: Group housing and age-dependent juvenile hormone (JH) jointly increase the expression of the male-specific proteins from fruitless (fruM), which is a master gene for male courtship behaviors (Peng et al., 2021; Sato et al., 2019; Yamamoto and Koganezawa, 2013), in the Or47b-expressing ORNs (Hueston et al., 2016; Sethi et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies on fruM expression in Or47b ORNs.

claim: Courtship levels in single-housed wild-type males are equal to or stronger than those in group-housed males.
source: Notably, courtship levels in single-housed (SH) wild-type males are equal to Dankert et al., 2009; Pan and Baker, 2014, in some cases, even stronger than those in group-housed (GH) males (Dankert et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies comparing courtship levels between housing conditions.

claim: Group housing decreases excitability of the courtship-promoting P1 neurons.
source: In fact, group housing decreases excitability of the courtship-promoting P1 neurons (Inagaki et al., 2014), which express both terminal genes in the sex determination hierarchy, fru and doublesex (dsx).
evidence: Supported by citation to Inagaki et al., 2014 study.

claim: Social experience shapes fighting strategies in male Drosophila.
source: Here, we found that social experience shapes the fighting strategies of male flies, in which GH males tend to reduce the low-intensity lunging and increase the high-intensity tussling.
evidence: Supported by experimental data throughout the study comparing single-housed and group-housed males.

claim: The two forms of fighting (lunging and tussling) are mediated by distinct sensory and central neurons.
source: We further showed that the two forms of fighting are mediated by distinct sensory and central neurons.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing different neurons control lunging versus tussling.

claim: The frequency of lunging decreases from 7-day-old to 14-day-old males.
source: It is important to note that the frequency of lunging decreases while the frequency of tussling increases from 7-day-old to 14-day-old males, suggesting a shift in fighting strategy with age.
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing different age groups.

claim: The mating advantage gained through social enrichment can offset the mating disadvantage associated with aging.
source: Interestingly, we found that the mating advantage gained through social enrichment can even offset the mating disadvantage associated with aging.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing 21-day-old group-housed males outcompete 14-day-old single-housed males.

claim: Or47b-dependent tussling is promoted by social enrichment with either male or female flies.
source: Unlike the Or67d-dependent lunging, which is primarily male-induced and socially inhibited, the Or47b-dependent tussling is promoted by social enrichment with either male or female flies.
evidence: Inferred from the known properties of Or47b neurons responding to pheromones common to both sexes and being enhanced by social enrichment.

claim: Female flies increase aggression towards mating pairs or mated females, depending on Or47b and Or67d, respectively.
source: Recently, it has been found that female flies increase aggression towards mating pairs or mated females, depending on Or47b and Or67d, respectively (Gaspar et al., 2022; Wan et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent studies on female aggression.

claim: There are ~60 pairs of dsx-expressing pC1 neurons in male flies.
source: In male flies, there are ~60 pairs of dsx-expressing pC1 neurons, including the well-characterized P1a neurons that also express fruM (Asahina, 2018; Jiang and Pan, 2022); however, there are only three pairs of pC1SS2 neurons that specifically express dsx but not fruM and are crucial for the high-intensity tussling in males.
evidence: Supported by citations to studies characterizing pC1 neurons.

claim: There are only three pairs of pC1SS2 neurons that specifically express dsx but not fruM.

evidence: Supported by experimental characterization of pC1SS2 neurons.

claim: pC1SS2 neurons are crucial for high-intensity tussling in males.

evidence: Supported by experimental data showing pC1SS2 neurons specifically promote tussling.

claim: P1a neurons promote both male courtship and aggression.
source: P1a neurons promote both male courtship and aggression (Hoopfer et al., 2015; Zhao et al., 2024), whereas pC1SS2 neurons specifically promote aggression but not courtship.
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on P1a neuron function.

claim: pC1SS2 neurons specifically promote aggression but not courtship.
source: P1a neurons promote both male courtship and aggression (Hoopfer et al., 2015; Zhao et al., 2024), whereas pC1SS2 neurons specifically promote aggression but not courtship.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing pC1SS2 activation does not affect courtship.

claim: dsx-positive pC1 neurons, rather than fruM-positive pC1 neurons, are crucial for male aggression.
source: That tussling-promoting pC1SS2 neurons specifically express dsx but not fruM is also consistent with a previous finding that dsx-positive pC1 neurons, rather than fruM-positive pC1 neurons, are crucial for male aggression (Koganezawa et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Koganezawa et al., 2016 study.

claim: The anatomical features of pC1SS2 neurons are highly similar to the male-specific aggression-promoting (MAP) neurons.
source: Moreover, the anatomical features of pC1SS2 neurons are highly similar to the male-specific aggression-promoting (MAP) neurons identified previously (Chiu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chiu et al., 2021 study and anatomical comparison.

claim: Visual stimuli amplify P1 activation and related behaviors.
source: These results align with previous findings that visual stimuli amplify P1 activation and related behaviors (Hindmarsh Sten et al., 2021; Kohatsu and Yamamoto, 2015; Pan et al., 2012), and visual stimulation is important for male aggression (Duistermars et al., 2018; Ramin et al., 2014; Schretter et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies on visual stimulation effects.

claim: Visual stimulation is important for male aggression.
source: These results align with previous findings that visual stimuli amplify P1 activation and related behaviors (Hindmarsh Sten et al., 2021; Kohatsu and Yamamoto, 2015; Pan et al., 2012), and visual stimulation is important for male aggression (Duistermars et al., 2018; Ramin et al., 2014; Schretter et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on visual stimulation and aggression.

claim: Male lunging is induced after P1a activation.
source: Male lunging is induced after P1a activation, whereas male tussling is induced during pC1SS2 activation.
evidence: Supported by optogenetic activation experiments showing temporal differences.

claim: Male tussling is induced during pC1SS2 activation.
source: Male lunging is induced after P1a activation, whereas male tussling is induced during pC1SS2 activation.

claim: P1a neurons may not directly regulate aggression but instead induce a persistent state that promotes aggression in general.
source: These results suggest that P1a neurons may not directly regulate aggression but instead induce a persistent state that promotes aggression in general, while pC1SS2 neurons may play a more direct role in mediating tussling.
evidence: Inferred from the temporal dynamics of P1a-induced behaviors and previous studies on P1a function.
